title: Virtual memory management (Linux)
summary: Linux virtual memory: each process has a virtual address space (mm_struct) containing VMAs (Virtual Memory Areas). VMAs describe contiguous regions of virtual memory (code, data, heap, stack, mmap'd files). Page tables map virtual pages to physical frames. Page faults trigger: minor (page in page cache) or major (disk I/O). Swap: anonymous pages can be swapped to disk. OOM killer: kills processes when memory is exhausted.

structure.meaning: Memory descriptor: list of VMAs, page table root (pgd), mmap base, brk (heap end), start/end of code/data/stack, etc.
Virtual memory area: start/end addresses, flags (read/write/exec/shared), file backing (if mmap'd), operations (fault, page_mkwrite, etc.).
Minor fault: page in page cache (fast). Major fault: read from disk (slow). Invalid access: SIGSEGV.
Heap, stack, anonymous mmap. Backed by swap (if configured) or zero page.
mmap'd files. Backed by page cache (file content in memory). Dirty pages written back to file.
Anonymous pages can be swapped to disk (swap partition/file). LRU-based eviction.
When memory is exhausted, kills the process with highest 'badness' score (memory usage, runtime, niceness).
Map files or anonymous memory into address space. Flags: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE, MAP_ANONYMOUS, MAP_FIXED.
Change protection (read/write/exec) of a memory region.

notes: Virtual memory provides isolation between processes and overcommitment of physical memory.
Page tables are managed by the kernel; user space accesses memory through virtual addresses.
Copy-on-write (COW) shares pages between processes until one writes (then copies).
Transparent huge pages (THP) automatically use 2MB pages for large allocations.
Memory overcommit: kernel allows allocating more virtual memory than physical RAM (OOM killer handles exhaustion).
